explanations.answer: Fifty men to run ahead of him
explanations.explanation: That's it, friend. Absalom, King David's son, gets a chariot, horses and fifty men running out front. Fifty! I think those fellas had a lot of cardio ahead of them, and I get winded just stamping a batch.

explanations.answer: Four hundred men to go up with him
explanations.explanation: Four hundred is a real number in David's story, but it's not this one. About four hundred men gathered around David when he was hiding out from Saul, Israel's earlier king (1 Samuel 22:2). Here, Absalom, David's son, has fifty men running ahead of him. That's a big entrance, just a smaller crowd.

explanations.answer: Six hundred men to march with him
explanations.explanation: Six hundred shows up in David's life too, when he and his men, about six hundred, left Keilah (1 Samuel 23:13). But that's a different story. In this passage, Absalom, David's son, has fifty men to run ahead of him. Fifty is plenty when they're all sprinting in front of your chariot.

Right on the money. Absalom calls out, "What city are you from?" It sounds like small talk, and I think that's the point. Notice he's making sure every grievance-bringer stops and chats with him first.
The text says otherwise, friend. Absalom calls out to the person and asks, "What city are you from?" That's the question he opens with. It's simple, and it gets people talking.

Close, but he says the opposite. Absalom tells the man, "Look, your claims are good and right, but the king has no deputy to hear you." He doesn't call the claims weak. He tells the man he's right, and that's what makes this so smooth.
That's right. Absalom says, "Look, your claims are good and right…" Nobody's getting told they're wrong here. I tell you, a man who hears "you're right" first will listen to whatever comes after.

explanations.answer: The king has no deputy to hear him
explanations.explanation: You got it, baker. Absalom says, "…the king has no deputy to hear you." He tells the man his claims are good, then points at a gap in the king's setup. And look who just happens to be standing there at the gate.

explanations.answer: The king's judges have been bribed
explanations.explanation: The text never says that, friend. No bribes come up anywhere in these verses. What Absalom says is that the king has no deputy to hear the man. That's the whole complaint he offers.

explanations.answer: The king is busy fighting a war
explanations.explanation: There's no war mentioned in these verses. Absalom says the king has no deputy to hear the man's claims. That's the only problem he names, and he names it with a smile.

Judge is right. Absalom says, "If only someone would appoint me judge in the land…" Then he adds that everyone with a grievance or dispute could come to him, and he would give them justice. I notice the job he wishes for is exactly the one he was just saying the king's missing.
Priest isn't the word. Absalom wishes someone would appoint him judge in the land. He wants to be the one hearing grievances and disputes. That's a job for the gate, not for the altar.

Commander is a good guess for a man with a chariot, but no. Absalom says he wishes someone would appoint him judge in the land. He wants people with a grievance or dispute to come to him, and he says he would give them justice. This speech is about sitting down and hearing cases, not leading troops.

explanations.answer: Takes hold of him and kisses him
explanations.explanation: That's the one. When anyone approaches to bow down, Absalom reaches out his hand, takes hold of him and kisses him. Imagine going to bow and getting pulled in for a kiss instead. I think a man would walk away from that feeling pretty important.

explanations.answer: Lets him bow and walks away
explanations.explanation: Walking away would be the opposite of what he does. The text says Absalom reaches out his hand, takes hold of the man and kisses him. He stops the bow and pulls the man close. That's the whole move.

explanations.answer: Has his runners push him back
explanations.explanation: No pushing in this passage, friend. Absalom reaches out his hand himself, takes hold of the man and kisses him. His fifty runners are out front of his chariot, not shoving people around. His whole approach here is warm, not rough.

Hearts it is. The text says, "In this way he stole the hearts of the men of Israel." He didn't take anything with his hands except a hand to hold and a kiss. The stealing happened somewhere much deeper, and nobody noticed.
No flocks went missing here, friend. The text says Absalom stole the hearts of the men of Israel. Nobody counted sheep and came up short. What he took couldn't be counted at all.

Not the land, though that's a fair guess for a man wanting to rule. The text says Absalom "stole the hearts of the men of Israel." The ground stayed right where it was. It was the people's loyalty that moved.

Right! Absalom says he made the vow while living in Geshur of Aram, a place outside Israel. He says he promised that if the LORD brought him back to Jerusalem, he would worship the LORD in Hebron. That's what he tells the king, anyway.

Tekoa is a real place in the story, but not here. Joab, David's commander, sent for a wise woman from Tekoa (2 Samuel 14:2). Absalom says he made his vow in Geshur of Aram. Same family drama, different town.

Gath comes up in David's own life, when he went to Achish, king of Gath (1 Samuel 21:10). But Absalom says he made his vow in Geshur of Aram. That's the place he names to the king. I have to say, I get mixed up with place names too, and I had one address for years.
True, friend. The king answers, "Go in peace." Then Absalom gets up and goes to Hebron. David says yes without any trouble.
The text says David agrees. After Absalom asks, the king says, "Go in peace." Absalom then gets up and goes to Hebron. There's no argument and no pushback, just a peaceful yes.

That's the message. The spies are told, "When you hear the sound of the horn, you are to say, 'Absalom reigns in Hebron!'" So a trip that began as a vow ends with a horn and a new king announced across the tribes. I think that's a big gap between what he told David and what he sent out.
That's the opposite of the plan. The spies are told to say, "Absalom reigns in Hebron!" David isn't named in the message at all. It's about a new king in a different city.
That would be a fine thing to shout, but it's not what Absalom's message says. The spies are told to say, "Absalom reigns in Hebron!" The horn is the signal, and Absalom's name is the announcement.

Not quite, friend. The text says the two hundred men from Jerusalem went along innocently, "for they knew nothing about the matter." They were invited as guests, so they came as guests. They had no idea what Absalom's plan was.

Right. The two hundred men from Jerusalem were invited as guests, and they "went along innocently, for they knew nothing about the matter." They thought they were going to a worship trip. Poor fellas, I think they'd have packed differently if they knew.

Sacrifices is right. While Absalom is offering the sacrifices, he sends for Ahithophel the Gilonite, David's counselor, to come from his hometown of Giloh. The sacrifices are happening, and in the middle of them Absalom sends for the counselor. That's a lot going on at one altar.

Firstfruits is a real offering in the Law, but it's not named here. The text says Absalom sends for Ahithophel, David's counselor, while he's offering the sacrifices. Ahithophel is from the town of Giloh. The word that fits the blank is sacrifices.

Incense isn't mentioned in these verses, friend. The text says Absalom is offering the sacrifices when he sends for Ahithophel the Gilonite, David's counselor. So the word for the blank is sacrifices. Nothing in the passage is burning but the plan.

That's right. The text says, "So the conspiracy gained strength, and Absalom's following kept increasing." Ahithophel, David's counselor, gets called in, and the crowd keeps growing. I think the king should be getting nervous about now.

It goes the other way, friend. The text says the conspiracy gained strength and Absalom's following kept increasing. Nobody is walking away from him in these verses. The line is getting longer, not shorter.

No split in this passage. The text says the conspiracy gained strength and Absalom's following kept increasing. One growing group, all behind Absalom. It's not two teams, it's one big and growing one.
